strengths: AugSub provides a simple, technically coherent way to combine ordinary supervised training with stronger regularization through shared-weight self-distillation. It requires no additional inference-time parameters or computation, and the same 50% masking ratio works across substantially different training recipes.

The central ImageNet results are convincing. Table 3 reports gains of 0.6–0.7 percentage points across ViT-S through ViT-H at 400 epochs, with improvements persisting at 800 epochs. Repeated runs strengthen this evidence: Table A.2 reports 84.08 ± 0.02 for ViT-B AugMask versus 83.46 ± 0.04 for the baseline.

The paper meaningfully addresses additional training cost. In Table 6, ViT-B AugMask achieves 84.1% using 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% for longer baseline training using 26 GPU-days. These comparisons support a practical benefit beyond simply spending more computation.

Evaluation is broad, covering ResNet, Swin, several pretrained-model fine-tuning recipes, distribution shifts, segmentation, detection, and transfer learning. Particularly useful evidence includes ViT-H ImageNet-A improving from 51.9 to 58.3 and ADE20K improvements of 0.4–0.6 mIoU. This breadth makes a stronger case for acceptance despite the method's incremental conceptual novelty.

The equations and pseudocode communicate the implementation clearly. Appendix B documents training recipes, hardware, and architecture-specific masking choices, while Appendix A supplies repeated-run statistics for several central experiments. A code URL is also provided.
weaknesses: The advance over closely related methods is insufficiently established. Section 2 explicitly identifies Co-sub [21] as similar, yet provides no direct experimental comparison. Shared-weight submodels, perturbations, and self-distillation are established ingredients; extending the perturbation choices is useful, but does not by itself substantiate the stronger claim of a substantially more general framework.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed relaxed supervision adequately. Table 1 compares hard-label training on a perturbed pass against supervised full-view training plus perturbed-view distillation, changing both the training views and their targets. A two-pass baseline supervising both views with labels, together with a matched symmetric-consistency comparison, would distinguish the benefits of the proposed asymmetry from those of an additional training view.

The mechanistic explanation needs qualification, although the objective itself is coherent. Equation 3 contains no correctness gate, so regularization is not applied exclusively to successfully classified examples; confident incorrect predictions can also supervise the submodel. Stop-gradient blocks differentiation through the target, while shared parameters still receive submodel updates. Figure 3 supports smaller early submodel gradients, but does not establish the claimed per-example prioritization or protection of main-model convergence.

Some claims of broadly significant improvement exceed the evidence. Repeated-run results are supplied for selected experiments, but uncertainty is absent for small gains such as 0.1 points on BEiT v2 and Swin-T and 0.2–0.3 AP on COCO. Section 4.2 acknowledges that CLIP's best-epoch performance is unchanged. Table 10 also shows ViT-B CIFAR-100 falling from 91.9 to 89.6 when AugMask is added during fine-tuning, demonstrating a meaningful limitation to its plug-in applicability.

The efficiency evidence is strongest for token-dropping ViTs. Training overhead is approximately 1.5× there and 2× for hierarchical architectures. The ResNet comparisons in Table 6 change both recipe and actual GPU budget, and equivalent cost comparisons are not provided for Swin or BEiT v2. Consequently, the demonstrated ViT efficiency gains should not be generalized to every evaluated setting.
